title: A visual guide to the new US tariff wall
gist: After the Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs, the Trump administration rebuilt its tariff wall as a patchwork of Section 232 and Section 301 measures whose four-hundred pages of exemptions make effective rates diverge sharply from headline rates: Latin America under 3 percent, Brazil 16.4 percent versus a 37.5 percent headline, China 22.8 percent, and India down from 50 percent to 3.6 percent. The author argues US leverage over China has weakened to just 7.5 percentage points of escalation room, and that the pending Section 301 industrial excess capacity investigation, covering over 75 percent of US imports, is the real test still ahead.

insights.claim: The Trump administration's latest tariff regime is not a blanket duty but a patchwork of Section 232 national security tariffs, Section 301 tariffs, exemptions, carveouts, and bilateral deals.
insights.so_what: Sector and country exposure now has to be modeled line by line; no single headline rate describes a company's actual tariff burden.
insights.locator: The Trump administration’s latest iteration of the tariff wall
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: A new tariff layer has been added from a Section 301 investigation under the Trade Act of 1974 tied to forced labor import prohibitions.
insights.so_what: Forced-labor compliance has become a tariff-rate determinant, making supply chain auditing a direct cost lever rather than an ESG checkbox.
insights.locator: Now, the administration has added yet another layer
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: The result is a fragmented and uneven tariff landscape creating advantages for India, setbacks for Brazil, uncertainty for Europe, and confusion elsewhere.
insights.so_what: Relative tariff advantage, not absolute level, is the tradeable variable across emerging-market exporters.
insights.locator: The result is a fragmented and uneven tariff landscape
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: In contrast to the Liberation Day poster board, the new regime comes with a four-hundred-page notice of action whose overlapping blanket, country-specific, and special exemptions produce significantly different and mostly much lower effective rates despite identical announced rates.
insights.so_what: Headline rate versus effective rate is now the core analytical distinction; trading the announcement is trading the wrong number.
insights.locator: In sharp contrast to the poster board
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: Most Latin American countries will face an effective additional tariff rate of less than 3 percent because more than 60 percent of their imports are exempt from the Section 301 forced labor tariffs and they are not subject to the second Section 301 investigation on manufacturing overcapacity.
insights.so_what: Latin American exporters are the structural winners of this tariff round, a relative-value case versus Asian manufacturing exporters.
insights.locator: Most Latin American countries will face an effective additional tariff
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: The Latin America outcome aligns with the administration's Donroe doctrine of strengthening ties with and expanding US influence over the Western Hemisphere, but may prove shortsighted.
insights.so_what: Tariff policy is being used as hemispheric statecraft, which means rates for the region are politically anchored and less likely to rise.
insights.locator: This outcome aligns with the Trump administration’s “Donroe” doctrine
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: Without close supervision, low Latin American tariffs may provide a backdoor for lower-cost Chinese imports rather than strengthening US economic leverage.
insights.so_what: Transshipment through the Western Hemisphere is the leakage risk that would trigger the next round of rules-of-origin enforcement.
insights.locator: Without close supervision, lower tariffs may provide a backdoor
insights.speaker: mchalecki

themes.theme: Asia's low headline, high effective inversion

insights.claim: Countries with documented forced labor risks such as Bangladesh, Pakistan, Indonesia, and Cambodia kept headline tariff rates at 10 percent to honor their IEEPA-era deals, but received fewer exemptions, leaving Asian economies with some of the highest effective tariffs despite the lower headline rate.
insights.so_what: Apparel and light-manufacturing exporters in South and Southeast Asia are more exposed than headline numbers suggest, an underpriced margin risk for their US importers.
insights.locator: In Asia, USTR faced a difficult balancing act
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: Structuring exemptions rather than headline rates makes the actual tariff more aligned with traditional forced labor concerns and therefore easier to legally defend than the announced rate suggests.
insights.so_what: Legal durability of these tariffs is higher than the IEEPA regime that was struck down, so pricing in a judicial reversal is riskier this time.
insights.locator: This structure means the actual rate is more aligned
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: The Turnberry deal's 15 percent tariff ceiling for most EU exports appears to hold under the current Section 301 regime when the most-favored-nation rate is taken into account, but additional Section 301 tariffs would push the US dangerously close to breaching it.
insights.so_what: A breach of the 15 percent cap would put the entire US-EU trade agreement at risk, a binary event for European exporters.
insights.locator: In last year’s Turnberry deal
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: A threatened Section 301 investigation into the EU's treatment of US tech firms could further erode European trust in the trade relationship.
insights.so_what: Digital regulation is becoming a tariff trigger, linking EU tech enforcement actions to goods-trade risk for European industrials.
insights.locator: After threatening another Section 301 investigation
insights.speaker: mchalecki

themes.theme: Brazil and China: headline versus effective

insights.claim: Brazil faces a cumulative 37.5 percent headline tariff comprising 12.5 percent from the forced labor Section 301 investigation and 25 percent from a separate Section 301 investigation, but exemptions cut the effective Section 301 rate to roughly 16.4 percent.
insights.so_what: The Brazil headline overstates the burden by more than half, so the market reaction to the announced rate likely overshot.
insights.locator: The headline tariff on Brazilian imports
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: China's effective rate is 22.8 percent, higher than Brazil's, because Chinese imports also carry Section 301 tariffs dating back to 2018 and receive far fewer exemptions.
insights.so_what: China remains the most tariffed major supplier on an effective basis, sustaining the incentive for supply chain relocation.
insights.locator: In practice, the effective Section 301 tariff rate is closer to 16.4 percent
insights.speaker: mchalecki

themes.theme: The US has lost leverage over China

insights.claim: The announced 12.5 percent tariff on Chinese imports raises China's effective tariff rate by 6.4 percentage points, and with Beijing signaling it will tolerate no more than a 20 percent total rate, Washington has only 7.5 percentage points of negotiating space left.
insights.so_what: A quantified escalation ceiling: 7.5 percentage points is the entire remaining US tariff runway before Beijing retaliates.
insights.locator: By announcing a 12.5 percent tariff on Chinese imports
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: With a record $1.2 trillion trade surplus in 2025 and other major partners including the EU, Japan, and Vietnam also facing additional tariffs, another 7.5 percentage point increase is unlikely to deter China, so the US negotiating position has weakened.
insights.so_what: The explicit conclusion is that US leverage has fallen, arguing against expectations of a favorable US-China trade deal.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, China continues to hold a strong hand
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: China will be the ultimate test of the administration's new tariff regime.
insights.so_what: Watch the China track as the determinant of whether the post-IEEPA architecture holds or escalates.
insights.locator: China will be the ultimate test
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: India has gone from one of the highest effective tariff rates to one of the lowest, falling from 50 percent under IEEPA to an additional effective rate of just 3.6 percent.
insights.so_what: The single largest relative tariff improvement in the new regime, a material competitiveness gain for Indian exporters versus Asian peers.
insights.locator: India has gone from having one of the highest effective tariff rates
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: India secured its reprieve by doubling down on negotiations after the Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs and by updating its trade policy to ban imports made with forced labor, aligning with the corresponding Section 301 investigation.
insights.so_what: A replicable playbook: aligning domestic forced-labor rules with the US investigation buys exemptions, so expect other exporters to copy it.
insights.locator: Much of this reversal is due to New Delhi doubling down
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: India's reprieve could be short-lived because it remains subject to the industrial excess capacity investigation and could face steep secondary tariffs under the proposed Russia sanctions bill.
insights.so_what: Indian exporter outperformance carries two identifiable reversal triggers, both with visible legislative and regulatory timelines.
insights.locator: Yet India’s reprieve could be short-lived
insights.speaker: mchalecki

themes.theme: The next phase is excess capacity

insights.claim: The current patchwork marks only the first phase of the post-IEEPA tariff wall, with the next phase set in motion by the pending Section 301 investigation into industrial excess capacity.
insights.so_what: Treat current rates as an interim equilibrium; the excess capacity ruling is the next scheduled repricing event.
insights.locator: The patchwork of Section 232 national security tariffs
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: The pending industrial excess capacity investigation targets many of the largest suppliers to the US market and covers more than 75 percent of total imports.
insights.so_what: Three quarters of US import value is exposed to a single pending decision, making it the dominant near-term trade risk for import-dependent margins.
insights.locator: The next phase will be set in motion
insights.speaker: mchalecki

insights.claim: The excess capacity investigation's outcome will determine both how much higher tariffs climb and which countries take the biggest hit, so the real test of the post-IEEPA strategy is still to come.
insights.so_what: Country-level tariff rankings are not yet settled; avoid locking in relative-country trade positioning before this ruling.
insights.locator: The investigation’s outcome will determine
insights.speaker: mchalecki
